lines.text: Why do calcium and barium fizz in water while magnesium scarcely does? The same two outer electrons drive their reactions, but become easier to remove down the group.

Group two metals form M two plus ions. With oxygen they form oxides, for example two M g of s plus O two gas gives two M g O solid. With cold water they form hydroxides and hydrogen, for example C a solid plus two H two O liquid gives C a open bracket O H close bracket two aqueous plus H two gas. Magnesium reacts only very slowly with cold water but with steam forms M g O and H two. With dilute hydrochloric acid they form chlorides and hydrogen, M g of s plus two H C l aqueous gives M g C l two aqueous plus H two gas. With dilute sulfuric acid they form sulfates and hydrogen, M g of s plus H two S O four aqueous gives M g S O four aqueous plus H two gas. An insoluble sulfate coating may slow the reaction. Water reactions become more vigorous from magnesium to barium.
The trend follows greater shielding and atomic radius down Group two, losing the two outer electrons becomes easier.
Oxygen gives a white metal oxide. Water gives hydroxide and hydrogen. Dilute hydrochloric or sulfuric acid gives salt and hydrogen. Cold water reactivity rises from magnesium to barium.
Why does calcium release hydrogen from cold water faster than magnesium, and what balanced equation describes calcium's reaction?
A white oxide can vanish in water without fizzing, a white carbonate fizzes in acid. Identifying the starting compound tells you which products to expect.

Group two oxides are basic and react with water to give hydroxides, B a O solid plus H two O liquid gives B a open bracket O H close bracket two aqueous. Hydroxides dissolve to different extents, making alkaline solutions, carbonates do not appreciably react with water alone. Oxides and hydroxides neutralise dilute hydrochloric or sulfuric acid to make the chloride or sulfate and water, for example M g O solid plus H two S O four aqueous gives M g S O four aqueous plus H two O liquid and C a open bracket O H close bracket two aqueous plus two H C l aqueous gives C a C l two aqueous plus two H two O liquid. Carbonates with either dilute acid make salt, carbon dioxide and water, M g C O three solid plus two H C l aqueous gives M g C l two aqueous plus C O two gas plus H two O liquid and C a C O three solid plus H two S O four aqueous gives C a S O four solid plus C O two gas plus H two O liquid. Insoluble sulfate may coat a carbonate and slow its reaction.
These are acid base reactions. The carbonate produces water as well as carbon dioxide, so its products differ from a metal plus acid.

Oxide plus water gives hydroxide, without gas. Oxide or hydroxide plus acid gives salt and water. Carbonate plus acid gives salt, carbon dioxide and water. Carbonates show no appreciable reaction with water alone.
Why does barium oxide dissolve without bubbles in water, while magnesium carbonate bubbles in hydrochloric acid?
Heating a Group two carbonate or nitrate reveals a dependable product pattern, the temperature needed also tells you how stable the compound is.

On heating, a Group two carbonate gives the oxide and carbon dioxide, C a C O three solid gives C a O solid plus C O two gas. ay Group two nitrate gives the oxide, brown nitrogen dioxide and oxygen, two C a open bracket N O three close bracket two solid gives two C a O solid plus four N O two gas plus O two gas. The nitrate equation needs two formula units to avoid a fractional oxygen coefficient. Thermal stability of both carbonates and nitrates increases from magnesium to barium. The larger cations lower down the group have lower charge density and polarise the large anions less, so more heat is required to decompose them.
This same change in cation size helps explain why the metals react more readily even though their salts become harder to decompose.
Carbonate heat, oxide plus carbon dioxide. Nitrate heat, oxide plus nitrogen dioxide plus oxygen. Both thermal stabilities increase down Group two.
Write the balanced equation for heating magnesium nitrate and predict whether barium nitrate needs more or less heat.
A trend lets you predict the behaviour of an unfamiliar Group two element from its position, but each property needs the correct direction.

From magnesium to barium, atomic radius and shielding increase and the outer electrons are lost more easily. Thus metal reactions with oxygen, cold water and dilute acids tend to become more vigorous, though an insoluble sulfate layer can affect an acid observation. Their oxides form basic hydroxides with water, oxides and hydroxides neutralise acids, and carbonates release carbon dioxide with acids. Both nitrates and carbonates become more thermally stable down the group, so higher decomposition temperatures are required. Hydroxides become more soluble, whereas sulfates become less soluble. Use these directions to predict observations, precipitates and comparative reaction temperatures. Metal melting points are irregular, so use supplied data instead of claiming a smooth trend.
Prediction combines the reaction patterns with the separate solubility and thermal stability trends.
Metal reactivity increases down the group. Carbonate and nitrate thermal stability increases. Hydroxide solubility increases, sulfate solubility decreases. Metal melting points are irregular.
Predict how strontium compares with calcium in its cold water reaction, carbonate decomposition and hydroxide solubility.
Two barium compounds behave very differently in water, its hydroxide can give a strongly alkaline solution, while its sulfate forms a white precipitate.

State the two opposite solubility trends separately. The solubility of Group two hydroxides increases down the group from magnesium hydroxide to barium hydroxide. The solubility of Group two sulfates decreases down the group from magnesium sulfate to barium sulfate. Magnesium hydroxide is only slightly soluble, barium hydroxide is considerably more soluble. Magnesium sulfate is soluble, while barium sulfate is very sparingly soluble. Thus a saturated barium hydroxide solution can have a higher p H than a saturated magnesium hydroxide solution, and mixing barium ions with sulfate ions gives a white barium sulfate precipitate.
Use solubility to decide whether a product remains dissolved or appears as a precipitate in the reactions of oxides, hydroxides and acids.
Hydroxide solubility increases from magnesium to barium. Sulfate solubility decreases from magnesium to barium. Barium sulfate is a white, very insoluble solid.

In one breath.
Group two metals become more reactive from magnesium to barium. Their nitrates and carbonates become more thermally stable, hydroxides become more soluble, while sulfates become less soluble.
Key ideas.

The Group two elements magnesium, calcium, strontium and barium form M two plus ions. Their outer electrons are lost more easily down the group because distance and shielding increase. Their reactions with water become faster, magnesium reacts only very slowly with cold water, calcium, strontium and barium react increasingly vigorously. Oxygen produces a white oxide, for example two M g of s plus O two gas gives two M g O solid. Water gives a hydroxide and hydrogen, for example C a solid plus two H two O liquid gives C a open bracket O H close bracket two aqueous plus H two gas. Magnesium reacts with steam more readily than cold water, forming magnesium oxide and hydrogen. With dilute hydrochloric acid, M g of s plus two H C l aqueous gives M g C l two aqueous plus H two gas, dilute sulfuric acid similarly gives the sulfate and hydrogen. An insoluble sulfate coating can slow a reaction.

Group two oxides are basic. An oxide plus water forms a hydroxide, B a O solid plus H two O liquid gives B a open bracket O H close bracket two aqueous. White barium oxide disappears into a colourless alkaline solution, there are no gas bubbles. Magnesium oxide and magnesium hydroxide are only slightly soluble. An oxide or hydroxide plus dilute hydrochloric or sulfuric acid gives a salt and water, such as M g O solid plus H two S O four aqueous gives M g S O four aqueous plus H two O liquid and C a open bracket O H close bracket two aqueous plus two H C l aqueous gives C a C l two aqueous plus two H two O liquid. Carbonates do not appreciably react with water alone. With dilute acid they produce salt, water and carbon dioxide, M g C O three solid plus two H C l aqueous gives M g C l two aqueous plus C O two gas plus H two O liquid.

On heating, Group two carbonates decompose, C a C O three solid gives C a O solid plus C O two gas. Nitrates form oxide, brown nitrogen dioxide and oxygen, two C a open bracket N O three close bracket two solid gives two C a O solid plus four N O two gas plus O two gas. Both nitrate and carbonate thermal stabilities increase down the group. A larger M two plus ion has lower charge density and polarises the anion less, so decomposition takes more heat.

The group two hydroxide solubility trend is upward from magnesium to barium, the group two sulfate solubility trend is downward. Thus B a open bracket O H close bracket two readily forms an alkaline solution, whereas B a S O four is nearly insoluble. These opposite trends predict precipitates and the p H of saturated hydroxide solutions. Melting points of the metals do not follow a simple smooth trend, so use supplied data for precise physical property predictions. For example, approximate melting points are magnesium six hundred and fifty degrees C, calcium eight hundred and forty two degrees C, Sr seven hundred and seventy seven degrees C and barium seven hundred and twenty seven degrees C. At seven hundred degrees C, magnesium has melted while calcium, strontium and barium remain solid, assuming the same pressure and no chemical reaction. Compare the temperature with each supplied melting point rather than assuming a smooth trend down the group.
Method.
Identify whether the starting material is metal, oxide, hydroxide, carbonate or nitrate.
Choose the reaction pattern, metal plus acid gives hydrogen, oxide or hydroxide neutralises acid, carbonate plus acid gives carbon dioxide and water, heat gives the decomposition products above.
Balance metal atoms, then the polyatomic ions, then hydrogen and oxygen. Check state symbols and whether a sulfate precipitates.
Worked example.

Predict and balance the products when magnesium carbonate reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid. Carbonate plus acid gives salt, carbon dioxide and water. Magnesium needs two chloride ions. M g C O three solid plus two H C l aqueous gives M g C l two aqueous plus C O two gas plus H two O liquid. Check, one magnesium, one C, three O, two H and two chlorine on each side.
Traps.
Trap, Oxide plus water effervesces. Why it's wrong, no gaseous product forms. Instead, describe hydroxide formation and any dissolving.
Trap, Carbonate plus acid gives only salt and carbon dioxide. Why it's wrong, water is also formed. Instead, include all three products.
Trap, Nitrate heating yields nitrogen monoxide. Why it's wrong, the Group two pattern produces nitrogen dioxide and oxygen. Instead, balance the N O two and O two together.
Trap, All Group two salts become more soluble down the group. Why it's wrong, sulfates show the reverse of hydroxides. Instead, state each trend separately.
Exam technique.

For Describe, give both observation and products. For Predict, name the trend and then apply it to the two elements. For Give an equation, balance it and include state symbols. If asked for a gas volume, first find moles from the balanced equation, then use the stated molar volume.
